query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a machine‐learning interatomic potential with analytic corrections for anharmonic vibrational and electron–vibration contributions can yield accurate fusion and high‐temperature free energy predictions at a substantially reduced computational cost compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary metallic systems (with extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys) in both solid and fluid states near their fusion temperatures.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an ML interatomic potential that is explicitly trained on ab initio data for both solid and fluid phases, then augmented with analytic models (e.g., Debye-Grüneisen for vibrational contributions and Sommerfeld-type corrections for electronic entropy) to capture anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling.
generation.conditions: The method is applied across a temperature range from roughly 0.8Tm to Tfusion and for compositions previously validated in elemental and binary studies; its extension to multicomponent alloys will be considered in regimes where the underlying free energy contributions remain comparable to those in simpler systems.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential forms the central model, while the analytic corrections serve as mediators that fine-tune the potential’s description of local bonding distortions and vibrational entropy, ensuring that both solid and fluid free energies are accurately reproduced.
generation.mechanism: By replacing the time-consuming explicit AIMD sampling with a fast ML-based evaluation (enhanced by analytic corrections), the free-energy landscape—incorporating anharmonic vibrational effects and electron–vibration coupling—is approximated with near ab initio fidelity, drastically reducing computational cost.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid approach should achieve a speedup of roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD workflows and outperform TOR-TILD in multicomponent systems, while maintaining free energy errors within ~10 meV/atom compared to high-fidelity ab initio calculations.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD methods for evaluating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for elemental and binary systems at high temperatures and be extendable to HEAs provided that the complexity of anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling does not introduce unforeseen discrepancies in the analytic corrections; validations should initially target systems with well-characterized vibrational and electronic entropy contributions.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the full transferability of the ML potential with analytic corrections to highly complex multicomponent systems and conditions with extreme anharmonic behavior that might exceed the range of the training data.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel evaluations of fusion/free energy curves using the new ML potential with analytic corrections and established explicit AIMD (or TOR-TILD) methods over a temperature range spanning from 0.8Tm to Tfusion for baseline elemental, binary, and selected high-entropy alloys. Benchmark both computational speed and free energy accuracy.
measurements: Computed free energy differences as a function of temperature for both solid and fluid phases
Error margins (meV/atom) between the ML-based free energies and ab initio reference values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be considered falsified if the ML approach fails to reduce the computational cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to AIMD, or if the free energy predictions deviate by more than ~10 meV/atom from high-fidelity ab initio values, leading to inaccurate prediction of phase-transition properties.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Vibrational contribution to formation free energy
cited_evidence.text: The vibrational contributions to the formation Gibbs free energy, ΔFvib, at 2000 K are listed in Table 1 for the six compositions synthesized as a single phase. The vibrational free energies, Fvib, are calculated using the Debye–Grüneisen model implemented in the AFLOW–Automatic GIBBS Library (AGL) module, using the Poisson ratio calculated with AFLOW–Automatic Elasticity Library (AEL). The average Fvib for the five-metal compositions are calculated, weighted according to the Boltzmann distribution at 2000 K. The vibrational contribution to the formation Gibbs free energy, ΔFvib, for each composition is obtained from the difference between its average Fvib and the average Fvib of its component binary carbides. ΔFvib at 2000 K ranges from ~0 meV/atom for HfNbTaTiWC5 to −31 meV/atom for HfNbTaTiVC5, which are significantly less than the total entropy contribution (mostly configurational plus vibrational) required to overcome the values of 50 meV/atom to 150 meV/atom for the formation enthalpy ΔHf. These results are in agreement with previous observations that the vibrational formation entropy is generally an order of magnitude smaller than the configuration entropy,.

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1.
